extracted.intended_audience: journalists, reporters and editors covering traumatic events and interviewing survivors
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for reporters and editors on covering traumatic events and interviewing survivors with sensitivity and ethical care, including interview planning, informed consent, question phrasing, inclusion, and self-care for journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand how trauma affects brain, memory and testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Trauma results from events or circumstances that are physically or emotionally harmful or life threatening and have lasting adverse effects on functioning; trauma can affect perception, judgment, memory and a person’s ability to vocalize events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that when the brain goes into survival mode eyewitnesses are notoriously unreliable; journalists may get an inaccurate or fragmented version of events immediately after a tragedy. Follow-up reporting months later, after sources have had time to heal, can produce more accurate accounts. Use SAMHSA and Dart Center definitions and resources to ground your understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Err on the side of overexplaining when getting informed consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Informed consent in trauma-informed reporting means informing sources about the nature of the story and having their consent to use their name and report on their experiences; do not assume sources understand journalistic terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be extremely clear about what 'on the record' or 'on background' mean. Offer options such as reviewing quotes or changing their mind before publication. In practice, allow survivors to review quoted excerpts when feasible (as Tamara Cherry did) to ensure ongoing consent and accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give power to survivors during the interview and storytelling process
rubrics_metrics.description: Modify usual journalistic rules when interviewing trauma survivors: allow more control for the source over questions, pacing and participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let sources know what questions you will ask and what they can decline to answer; consider sharing questions in advance or letting them choose which questions to answer. Ask survivors what they want to achieve by telling their story and respect those goals. Breaking typical rules (e.g., not showing questions beforehand) is acceptable to protect and empower survivors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan interviews to care for sources before, during and after
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a clear plan for how you will support and protect survivors throughout the interview process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let survivors pick the interview location so they feel safe; tell them the questions you plan to ask and ask if there are topics to avoid; check during the interview whether they want a break and ensure they are not reliving the event. At the end, thank them and explain how their interview will be used and when to expect the story. For remote interviews, follow guidance (e.g., Jo Healey) on handling sensitivity and logistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat victims with dignity and respect and properly identify yourself
rubrics_metrics.description: Basic interview behaviors are critical when working with trauma survivors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always treat victims with dignity and respect. Clearly identify yourself and your role. Never say 'I understand' or 'I know how you feel.' Avoid overwhelming the source with the hardest questions first. If a source reacts harshly, leave a contact number or card and explain they can contact you later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the question 'How do you feel?' — use less distressing alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: 'How do you feel?' is consistently reported by survivors as distressing and inappropriate and rarely yields coherent, useful answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer questions such as 'How are you now?', 'How did you experience that?' or 'What do you think about ...?' which invite reflection without demanding an immediate emotional inventory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use open-ended, source-led prompts and avoid interrogating emotionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Open-ended prompts let survivors control what they share and how they begin their story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask 'Where would you like to begin?' or 'Would you tell me what you are able to remember about your experience?' Avoid asking why a source is emotional or implying their reaction is inappropriate even if it seems disproportionate to you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure transparency and inclusion for later productions (podcasts, videos, series)
rubrics_metrics.description: When producing longer-form projects or retrospectives, keep survivors informed and offer opportunities to participate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If producing a podcast, video or printed story about a past crime or tragedy, make sure survivors are aware and extend the opportunity for their voice to be included; failing to do so can make them feel talked about 'behind their back' or surprised by coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid surprise/shock coverage and respect sources' sense of safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic practices that are normal for institutional figures may harm survivors if applied without adaptation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not 'stuff a microphone in someone’s face' or spring stories on survivors. Take time to introduce yourself, make eye contact, explain why you want to talk, take it slowly and do not rush—even in chaotic circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for and address journalists' own mental health and vicarious trauma
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting on traumatic events can negatively affect journalists' mental health; symptoms can range widely and include PTSD indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of signs such as inability to concentrate, feeling on edge or numb, inability to feel compassion, sleep problems, anger, or excessive substance use. Follow self-care recommendations: know your limits, take breaks, find a trusted colleague to talk with, cultivate hobbies/exercise/family time, and seek counseling if overwhelmed. Consult Dart Center resources and trainings (e.g., 'Tragedies & Journalists').

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground practice in established trauma-informed resources and style guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Use authoritative resources to define trauma-related terminology and best practices rather than relying on ad hoc approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to and apply guidance from sources like The Dart Center Style Guide for Trauma-Informed Journalism, Dart Center guides ('Trauma & Journalism', 'Tragedies & Journalists'), SAMHSA definitions, and other listed readings and training materials to inform terminology, interview techniques and newsroom policies.
